summary: Clarifies and gives guidelines for using the SIPS URI scheme in SIP, which asks for secure delivery. It also makes normative changes to SIP.

eli5.summary: A normal address delivers a letter. A SIPS address asks for a sealed, tamper-proof path. This explains when and how to ask.

questions: what is the sip last hop exception
subtitle: What a sips: address really promises in SIP, and the rules that stop proxies from quietly weakening it.

tldr.problem: The meaning of the SIPS URI scheme and of TLS in SIP was underspecified in RFC 3261 and confused implementers, and the last-hop exception left a hole in the promise of a secure path.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC says a SIPS URI means TLS on every hop up to the target, forbids downgrading SIPS to SIP and upgrading SIP to SIPS, deprecates the last-hop exception, and gives behavior rules for user agents, registrars, proxies and redirect servers.
tldr.outcome: It updates RFC 3261 and RFC 3608. It also warns that SIPS only asks for secure delivery and is not proof that a request was delivered securely.

today: RFC 5630 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2009 that updates RFC 3261 and RFC 3608. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why SIPS Needed Clarifying
sections.content:
The meaning and usage of the SIPS URI scheme and of Transport Layer Security (TLS) were underspecified in SIP (RFC 3261) and were a source of confusion for implementers. RFC 5630 provides clarifications and guidelines for SIPS, and it also makes normative changes to RFC 3261 and to RFC 3608.

Appendix A lists corrections to RFC 3261 needed to support the new text. One example is that a client MUST NOT automatically retry a request with a SIP URI when the original Request-URI used the SIPS scheme.
sections.eli5: People disagreed about what a secure-address label really meant. This RFC settles it and fixes a few mistakes in the older rulebook.

sections.title: TLS Models and the Last-Hop Problem
sections.content:
The RFC first describes two ways to use TLS in SIP. With server-provided certificates, only the server sends a certificate, so a user agent can authenticate its proxy. The user agent always opens the connection and keeps it alive, which also helps with NATs and firewalls, and RFC 5626 gives the standard way to do that. With mutual authentication, both sides send certificates. That is mostly used between servers, because setting up certificates for a wide population of user agents has proven impractical.

The RFC also explains that plain TLS with SIP URIs is a "best-effort" service, while SIPS is "TLS-only". The transport=tls URI parameter is deprecated, and UAs, proxies and redirect servers MUST NOT use it.

The original last-hop exception let the final hop from the target domain's proxy to the user agent skip TLS depending on local policy. It was written before RFC 5626, when the target device often could not accept a TLS connection. The RFC says the rationale was somewhat flawed and that RFC 5626 solves the problem better.
sections.eli5: There are two ways to lock a mailbag: only the post office shows ID, or both sides do. The old rules also let the very last step go unlocked, and that turned out to be a bad idea.

sections.title: What a SIPS URI Now Means
sections.content:
A SIPS URI means the resource is to be contacted securely, using TLS on each hop between the UAC and the remote UAS, not only up to the proxy of the target domain. The last-hop exception is deprecated for proxies forwarding to the last hop.

SIPS is different from just using TLS because it is a demand rather than a preference: if the network cannot comply, the request should fail instead of being delivered without TLS. It also works in many places a Require option tag would not, such as Contact, Route, Record-Route, business cards and HTML.

SIPS implies transitive trust. Proxies could cheat, so a SIPS Request-URI or To header is not proof that every hop was secured. The RFC says its meaning is not to be oversold and that there is no mechanism for end-to-end security indication in SIP.

A SIP and a SIPS URI that differ only in scheme, such as sip:bob@example.com and sips:bob@example.com, refer to the same resource.
sections.eli5: A SIPS label means use a locked bag the whole way, not just most of it. But it is a request, not a guarantee, because someone along the way could cheat.

sections.title: User Agent and Registrar Rules
sections.content:
A UAC or UAS that is given a SIPS URI MUST NOT change it to a SIP URI. If the Request-URI or top Route is SIPS, the Contact MUST be SIPS too. After a 416 or a 480 with warn-code 380, the UAC MUST NOT automatically retry with SIP, and SHOULD get user confirmation if it does.

To be reachable by SIPS, a UA MUST register with a SIPS Contact, and then requests to either its SIP or SIPS AOR are routed to it. A UA that does not want SIPS MUST register with a SIP Contact. A UA MUST NOT include both versions of the same Contact in one REGISTER.

A UAS that wants only SIP, or only SIPS, MUST reject the other with a 480 (Temporarily Unavailable) and SHOULD add a Warning with warn-code 380 "SIPS Not Allowed" or 381 "SIPS Required". Inconsistent URIs get a 400 (Bad Request).

Derived dialogs, such as a transfer made with REFER, MUST NOT effectively downgrade SIPS to SIP without explicit authorization. A registrar MUST treat AORs that differ only in scheme as equivalent and MUST reject with 400 a SIPS binding whose related URIs are not all SIPS.
sections.eli5: If you ask for the locked bag, nobody may quietly switch to an open one. If a mail carrier cannot comply, it says so, and only you get to decide whether to try the open bag.

sections.title: Proxy and Redirect Server Rules
sections.content:
A proxy MUST NOT use the last-hop exception. When it gets a SIPS Request-URI, it MUST forward only to a SIPS Request-URI, and if the target registered a plain SIP Contact it MUST NOT forward, rejecting with 480 and SHOULD add warn-code 380.

When a proxy gets a SIP Request-URI, it MUST NOT forward to a SIPS Request-URI. If the target registered a SIPS Contact, the proxy replaces the scheme with SIP and MUST use TLS to forward the request. Proxies SHOULD send SIP requests over TLS when they can set up or reuse a TLS connection.

If a downgrade or upgrade response such as a 3XX or 480 comes back, the proxy MUST NOT recurse on it and SHOULD forward the best response so that the UAC can decide. Using the outbound procedures of RFC 5626 is RECOMMENDED for UACs that cannot provide a certificate.

A redirect server is limited because no connection exists to the UAS beforehand. It MUST return a SIP Contact if the target registered a SIP Contact. It SHOULD return a SIPS Contact if the target registered one and TLS is usable.
sections.eli5: Mail sorters may not relabel a locked-bag letter as ordinary, or an ordinary letter as locked. If the rules cannot be followed, they send the letter back with a note.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Most of the document is itself security considerations for the SIPS URI. The RFC says the last-hop exception of RFC 3261 introduced significant potential vulnerabilities in SIP, which is why it is deprecated.

Section 26.4.4 of RFC 3261 on SIPS security also applies, as modified by Appendix A. The RFC adds that checks such as inspecting header fields or the History-Info header can be circumvented by proxies or B2BUAs that do not follow the rules. SIP Identity (RFC 4474) is mentioned as a better mechanism for an authenticated identity and domain-to-domain integrity.
sections.eli5: Closing the unlocked last step makes the route safer. But no label can stop a dishonest carrier, so important letters need extra proof.

sections.title: New Warning Codes
sections.content:
The RFC registers two warning codes in the Warning Codes (warn-codes) sub-registry of the SIP Parameters registry: 380 "SIPS Not Allowed" and 381 "SIPS Required".

They are carried in the Warning header of a 480 (Temporarily Unavailable) response to tell the sender why a request was refused because of the SIP or SIPS scheme.
sections.eli5: Two new reason stickers were added to the refusal slip: one says secure delivery is not allowed here, and the other says it is required.

items.label: SIPS Not Allowed
items.desc: Sent with a 480 when a request for SIPS cannot be delivered securely, so it cannot be downgraded.

items.label: SIPS Required
items.desc: Sent with a 480 when a SIP request would need to be upgraded to SIPS.
